sections.title: Introduction and Corrosion Mechanisms
sections.summary: Corrosion protection is required to ensure long-term durability of prestressed ground anchor tendons. Four main corrosion types for prestressing steel: general corrosion (uniform rust — generally minor if limited exposure); pitting corrosion (localized attack, can cause stress concentrations); hydrogen embrittlement (from hydrogen absorption in electrochemical reactions, catastrophic risk); and stress corrosion cracking (cracks develop under sustained stress with corrosive environments, catastrophic risk). Hydrogen embrittlement and stress corrosion cracking are the most critical failure modes for prestressing steel.
sections.body:
Protecting metallic components of the tendon against corrosion is necessary to assure adequate long-term durability. Corrosion protection includes physical barrier layers: anchorage covers, corrosion-inhibiting compounds, grout (primary protection for bond length), sheaths and encapsulations (unbonded length), and trumpets.

Corrosion types for prestressing steel: (1) General corrosion — thin uniform rust layer, negligible if limited exposure, not typically considered detrimental for light surface rust. (2) Pitting corrosion — localized, creates stress concentration points; more serious than general corrosion. (3) Hydrogen embrittlement — hydrogen atoms from electrochemical reactions diffuse into the metal lattice, causing internal fracture with little deformation; catastrophic failure mode for high-strength steel. (4) Stress corrosion cracking — develops under sustained stress with corrosive environment; also potentially catastrophic.

Anchors are most vulnerable to corrosion in highly aggressive soils, near stray electrical current sources, at anchorage transitions, and when corrosion protection barriers are incomplete or damaged.
key_points: Hydrogen embrittlement and stress corrosion cracking are catastrophic failure modes for prestressing steel
Pitting corrosion creates stress concentrations — more critical than uniform general corrosion
Light surface rust is not detrimental; heavily pitted bars must be rejected even if grout-tendon bond appears adequate

sections.title: Corrosion Protection Systems and Level Selection
sections.summary: Two corrosion protection classes per PTI (1996): Class I (encapsulated tendon) — all three zones protected by physical encapsulation plus grout; Class II (grout only) — grout is the primary barrier with no encapsulation. Selection by decision tree (Figure 63): permanent anchors in aggressive or unknown ground → Class I; permanent anchors in non-aggressive ground → Class II if consequences are not serious and higher protection cost is significant; otherwise Class I. SOE temporary anchors in non-aggressive ground → no protection required. Aggressivity assessed by pH, resistivity, chloride, and sulfate content testing.
sections.body:
Protection classes (Table 20, after PTI 1996):
- Class I (Encapsulated Tendon): Anchorage — trumpet + cover; Unbonded length — encapsulated individual grease-filled strand sheaths with common smooth sheath (or grout-filled smooth sheath); Bond length — corrugated or smooth high-density polyethylene (HDPE) or polypropylene sheath (encapsulation); provides a fully redundant double barrier against corrosion throughout anchor length.
- Class II (Grout Protected): Anchorage — trumpet + cover; Unbonded length — smooth sheath filled with grout; Bond length — grout provides the primary and only barrier; not encapsulated.

Selection by Figure 63 decision tree:
1. Permanent anchor: If ground is aggressive or aggressivity not known → Class I. If non-aggressive:
   - If consequences of failure are serious → Class I.
   - If consequences not serious: If cost for Class I is small → Class I; if cost significant → Class II.
2. Temporary SOE anchor: If ground is aggressive or unknown → Class II. If non-aggressive → no protection required.

Aggressivity of ground: Evaluate by pH, resistivity, chloride content, and sulfate content (chapter 3). Aggressive conditions include: pH ≤ 4 or pH ≥ 12; chloride > 100 ppm; sulfate > 200 ppm; resistivity < 2,000 ohm-cm. Areas near mining operations, chemical plants, or chemical storage may also be aggressive.

Corrosion of structural steel soldier beams: Corrosion protection typically by painting or other coatings. The use of weathering steel may be considered.
key_points: Class I (encapsulated): double barrier — encapsulation + grout; Class II: grout only
Decision tree: aggressive/unknown ground → Class I for permanent; non-aggressive + serious consequences → Class I
SOE anchors in non-aggressive ground: no corrosion protection required
Aggressivity criteria: pH ≤ 4 or ≥ 12; Cl > 100 ppm; SO4 > 200 ppm; resistivity < 2,000 ohm-cm
